core_contributions.title: Buffered Postgres CDC made safe: ordering, deletes, resets and slot hygiene
core_contributions.what: He built the pre-write CDC load-resolution layer (ordering guard, keep-highest dedupe, delete-enrichment verification, fail-closed flag) that unblocked buffered S3 ingress, then added buffered ingress itself, forced the v3 pipeline for buffered schemas, routed CDC snapshots through the buffer, and closed a long list of failure modes: reset races that wiped tables, truncates silently ignored, primary-key changes leaving stale rows, quiet runs letting WAL build up until the slot dropped, expired buffer files and ETag-based buffer deletion to stop double-counted billable rows.
core_contributions.why_it_matters: CDC is the path customers use for live Postgres replication into the warehouse. Each bug class here produced wrong data with no error (lost deletes, duplicated or stale rows), customer database WAL growth, or billing for rows that were never new.
core_contributions.outcome: 43 PRs mention CDC or replication slots (23 major), peaking in September (24). Deep reads score the core pieces at the top of his range: #82568 P=16.0, #90152 P=9.6, #105139 P=9.6, #108591 P=7.3. 12 major ws1 PRs landed in the single week of 2026-09-21 alone. No CDC PR was reverted.

core_contributions.title: Silent data-loss and billing fixes across SaaS and SQL sources
core_contributions.what: He fixed data that customers were losing or being charged for without knowing: Stripe webhook upserts overwriting complete invoice rows with partial payloads, Stripe basil API breakage and tie-breaking that left paid invoices open, Help Scout syncs missing conversation statuses, Postgres replica re-reads duplicating and dropping rows, xmin wraparound dropping rows, resumable syncs duplicating rows after worker rotations, a lost-update race that resurrected soft-deleted table links, and repartition rewrites that OOM-killed workers forever (an incident affecting 16 customers).
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Revenue analytics reads these Stripe tables directly, and a warehouse that silently duplicates or drops rows breaks every downstream join, insight and billing count without anyone seeing an error.
core_contributions.outcome: Five of these are deep-read at P=13.0 or higher (#98817, #118548, #123458, #93764 at 13.0; #86717 at 16.0). Two shipped as public changelog entries (Complete Help Scout conversation syncs, Keep Stripe data available). The replica re-read fix #93764 needed a same-week regression fix (see red flags).

core_contributions.title: Credential and injection hardening on source connections
core_contributions.what: A run of security fixes: escaping column names in the ClickHouse s3()/deltaLake() structure argument (expression injection), validating Google token_uri against Google's endpoints for BigQuery and then generalising the check across every Google Cloud key-file integration and export, pinning validated addresses against DNS rebinding for Redshift/MySQL/PlanetScale/Postgres, MySQL and database TLS certificate verification, and per-view edit checks closing an authorization bypass in data modeling.
core_contributions.why_it_matters: Warehouse sources accept customer-supplied hosts, key files and column names; each of these was a path to SSRF, credential exfiltration or query injection against PostHog infrastructure.
core_contributions.outcome: 8 security PRs, 7 major. #102485 applies one shared check across service-account, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, Firebase, BigQuery batch-export and warehouse paths (deep read P=7.8, L=2); #91115 deep read P=7.8.

calibration.note: He sits in the middle of the 20 on delivery (10th), quality rate (9th) and team leverage (10th of 19), and near the bottom on trust rank (19th). The overall 7 sits above the delivery percentile on purpose: the episode estimate compresses his many related CDC fixes, while major_episodes (p89.5) and changelog_prs (p94.4) show the work is unusually critical and visible, and the deep reads confirm V3 C3 customer data-loss fixes. The team grade of 5 matches the median leverage and low trust rank. The quality grade of 6 tracks the mid quality rate and is not higher because most of his critical PRs were never human-reviewed.

custom_analyses.question: Who actually signs off on his work, and how much of his quality record is peer-tested?
custom_analyses.why: He ships 232 PRs at an 88% AI co-authored share, yet only 80 human reviews were received on his PRs; first_pass_rate and changes_requested_rate are only meaningful if humans reviewed the critical PRs.
custom_analyses.finding: 94 human reviews on 75 PRs from 17 reviewers; Gilbert09 alone covers 50. Joining the pack's reviews.json to his PR list: 30 of 76 major PRs, 41 of 134 substantive and 4 of 19 routine had any human reviewer. The raw review records show the rest were approved by the stamphog bot (171 bot approvals on his PRs), and 221 of 223 review threads opened on his PRs came from bots. Major unreviewed examples include #98817, #118548, #90152, #102485 and #111998. The pattern is flat over time (14 of 43 in August, 29 of 85 in September, 31 of 103 in October).
custom_analyses.effect: quality 7 → 6 because the clean first-pass record covers only 32% of his PRs and two thirds of his major PRs had no human check; overall confidence lowered to medium.

insights.insight: His output is AI-assisted end to end: 88% of PRs are AI co-authored, most are approved by a bot reviewer, and part of his review commentary is labelled AI review. The resulting quality is good on average (0 reverts, Q mean 1.83) but all five follow-up-fixed PRs are AI co-authored, so the human checkpoint is the weak link, not the code generation.

He is the area's number-two author and Gilbert09's main review partner (205 PRs reviewed one way, 50 the other). His standing depends on that pairing: outside warehouse-sources he is barely requested and his trust rank is 19th of 20.

Counting PRs overstates the October burst and understates September. Roughly 30 alpha connector PRs landed 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-22, mostly substantive with no deep read, while the fewer September CDC PRs carry the highest-value work.

red_flags.flag: Five PRs were explicitly follow-up fixed by others within 14 days (peer.followup_fixed=5), all AI co-authored, including a duplicate-and-skip rows regression chain on Postgres full refresh (#93764 then #94379) and duplicated rows from the new Stripe balance-transaction sweep (#118547).
#116588: the deep-read quote for the Q score was not found in the source, so that PR's Q score is unverified.
46 of 76 major PRs merged with no human review, approved only by a bot; the low changes-requested rate does not cover them.

counter_evidence: His PR descriptions frame many changes as critical fixes, and the deep reads mostly agree (V3 C3 on several), but peer behaviour is weaker than the self-description: few people build on his files (52 downstream authors, p15.8), only 2 people request his review, and most critical PRs were never examined by a human, so their quality is asserted by tests and bots rather than shown by colleagues. Against the red flags: there are 0 reverts, the regressions were fixed within one to ten days, and he reviewed the fix to his own Stripe change. The trivial #116361 deep-read at P=13.0 is an outlier from scoring an admin-text change and should not be read as major delivery; similarly the stratified delivery estimate (1765) is inflated by the trivial stratum calibration gap (6.33), so the episode estimate (677) is the safer number.
